claims.text: Low-temperature annealing will increase the coercive field of magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Low-temperature annealing modifies the stress and defect structure of magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Modification of the stress and defect structure produces a more stable magnetic-domain configuration.
A more stable magnetic-domain configuration increases the coercive field.
The intervention is annealing at 200 °C for 2 hours.
The initial material may be either as-cast or already annealed.
Stress and defect structure will be characterized using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.
Annealing is predicted to increase coercive field by 20%, from 1000 Oe to 1200 Oe, relative to an as-cast matched baseline.
The as-cast baseline has a coercive field of 1000 Oe.
The coercivity-enhancing effect should hold for annealing temperatures below 300 °C and annealing times of 1–5 hours.
Prior studies have shown that annealing below 300 °C for 1–5 hours effectively modifies stress and defect structure in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
The effect is to be evaluated at room temperature and standard atmospheric pressure.
The exact relationship between annealing conditions and coercive-field increase is not well understood.
The hypothesis is falsified if the annealed alloy's coercive field is not at least 15% higher than the as-cast alloy's coercive field.

contradictions.description: The allowed initial state includes an already annealed material, but the stated matched baseline and comparison experiment use only an as-cast material, leaving the baseline undefined for the annealed-initial-state case.
The quantitative prediction is a 20% increase, whereas increases from 15% to below 20% would miss that prediction but would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
